The ADR primarily describes the choice of a modern technology stack for a simple application and experimentation purposes. It focuses on what technologies to use rather than any quality attribute of the system such as performance, security, or maintainability. Although it mentions some effort to monitor security alerts, the main decision is about the functional aspect of technology selection, not about improving security or other quality attributes explicitly.

The ADR focuses on client-side routing and generating HTML files with Open Graph Protocol meta tags to improve link previews in services like Slack. This primarily enhances the user experience when sharing and accessing specific images, which relates to Usability. Although there is mention of routing and deployment constraints, the core motivation is to improve how users interact with and share links to the system's content. Other categories like Compatibility or Portability are less relevant since the decision is not about interoperability or environment transfer, and Performance or Scalability are not the focus here.

The ADR focuses on improving the user experience by eliminating the intermediate redirect step, which reduces page load time and speeds up access to the pixel art gallery. This is primarily a performance improvement related to response time and user-perceived latency. Although usability is somewhat impacted, the core motivation is faster page loading rather than interface design or accessibility. Other categories like Maintainability or Security are not relevant here as the decision is about how the system delivers content efficiently.

The ADR focuses on maintaining valid URLs for pixel art entries even after renaming, ensuring that old URLs (aliases) remain functional and redirect to the canonical URL. This is primarily about interoperability and seamless integration with external references/bookmarks, which aligns with Compatibility. It is not primarily about performance, security, or maintainability, but about ensuring the system can work correctly with external systems and user expectations regarding URLs.

The ADR focuses on adopting TypeScript for static typing to catch errors at compile time and document interfaces, which primarily improves the ease of understanding, modifying, and maintaining the codebase. This aligns with Maintainability as it enhances code quality and reduces errors during development. There is no indication that the decision is primarily about runtime performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes.

The ADR describes the process of recording architectural decisions using a specific template. It focuses on documentation and process rather than any quality attribute of the system being built. There is no mention or implication of performance, security, maintainability, or any other quality attribute related to the system itself.

The ADR focuses on structuring the system as a Modular Monolith using Domain-Driven Design tactical patterns to divide the system into autonomous modules. This primarily addresses the ease of modification, modularity, and organization of the system, which are aspects of Maintainability. There is no mention or implication of performance, scalability, security, or other quality attributes as the main motivation. The decision is about how the system is organized internally to facilitate changes and understanding, not about what it does or how fast or secure it is.

The ADR focuses on choosing .NET Core and C# because .NET Core is a multi-platform framework that supports running the application on Windows, MacOS, and Linux. This indicates a primary concern with platform independence and environment neutrality, which aligns with Portability. Although the decision mentions language choice and experience, the key quality attribute is the ability to run the system across different operating systems. There is no indication that performance, security, or other attributes are the main drivers here.

The ADR focuses on dividing the system into autonomous modules to improve maintainability aspects such as modularity, readability, separation of concerns, and independent development. The primary motivation is to make the system easier to modify and evolve by structuring it into clear bounded contexts. Although complexity and communication between modules are mentioned, the core driver is maintainability rather than performance, scalability, or other attributes.

The ADR focuses on the architectural decision to reduce complexity and improve ease of change and configuration by having a single API module rather than multiple API projects. This primarily addresses maintainability aspects such as reducing complexity, simplifying configuration, and build time, which are related to how easy it is to modify and manage the system. There is no indication that performance, scalability, security, or other quality attributes are the main drivers here. The decision is about the structure and organization of the system for easier maintenance.

The ADR focuses on introducing a façade interface between the API and business modules to encapsulate module implementation details and simplify API communication. This primarily improves modularity and ease of change, which are aspects of Maintainability. The decision aims to make the system easier to modify and evolve without impacting the API, rather than improving performance, security, or other quality attributes.

The ADR focuses on applying the CQRS pattern to separate read and write models, which improves modularity and separation of concerns, making the system easier to modify and evolve. The emphasis is on structuring the system for clarity and maintainability rather than on performance, scalability, or other attributes. Although there are mentions of optimized models and processing, the primary motivation is to improve the system's organization and maintainability.

The ADR discusses a functional design decision about whether commands can return results or not, focusing on the behavior of command processing and immediate data return. It does not address how well the system performs, scales, secures, or maintains this behavior, but rather what the system does functionally. Although it mentions complexity as a consequence, the primary focus is on functional behavior rather than a quality attribute like Maintainability or Performance.

The ADR focuses on using a 2-layered architecture for read operations to improve performance by reducing overhead such as object mapping and querying the database almost immediately. The primary motivation is to achieve better response times and efficiency in query handling. Although maintainability aspects like simplicity and ease of understanding are mentioned, the main driver is performance improvement. There is no emphasis on scalability, security, or other quality attributes as the core rationale.

The ADR focuses on structuring the system using Clean Architecture to isolate domain logic, improve testability, readability, and reduce coupling. These aspects primarily relate to Maintainability, as they facilitate easier modification and understanding of the system. Although testability is mentioned, it is a consequence of the architectural layering rather than the primary focus on testing itself. Performance, Security, Scalability, and other categories are not the main drivers here.

The ADR focuses on structuring the system's domain model to encapsulate business logic using object-oriented principles like abstraction and encapsulation. This primarily improves the system's modifiability, encapsulation, and clarity of business rules, which are aspects of Maintainability. There is no explicit mention of performance, scalability, security, or other quality attributes as the main driver. Although testability is mentioned as somewhat decreased, the core decision is about design structure and ease of modification, not testing specifically. Therefore, Maintainability is the best fit.

The ADR focuses on using Domain-Driven Design tactical patterns to structure the domain model and business logic, which primarily improves the modularity, organization, and ease of modification of the system. It does not primarily address performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes. The decision is about how to organize and maintain the codebase effectively, which aligns with Maintainability.

The ADR focuses on how to handle business invariant violations in a way that improves code clarity and reduces complexity (less if/else statements), which relates to ease of modification and understandability of the system. The decision to use exceptions is motivated by maintainability concerns such as reducing boilerplate checks and centralizing error handling. Although performance impact is mentioned, it is considered irrelevant and not the primary driver. Security, reliability, or other quality attributes are not the main focus here.

The ADR focuses on choosing an event-driven asynchronous communication pattern between modules to achieve maximum autonomy and loose coupling. This approach supports modules scaling independently and handling increased load without blocking calls, which aligns with the quality attribute of Scalability. Although there is mention of complexity and eventual consistency, the primary motivation is to enable modules to scale and evolve independently rather than immediate performance or reliability concerns. Other categories like Maintainability or Performance are less fitting because the decision emphasizes decoupling and asynchronous communication rather than ease of change or optimization of response times.

The ADR focuses on choosing an in-memory event bus primarily motivated by performance considerations such as avoiding network communication and simplicity for efficient inter-modular asynchronous communication. Although other aspects like integration complexity and features are mentioned, the core decision is driven by performance trade-offs. It is not primarily about reliability, security, or maintainability, and scalability is only indirectly referenced as a future concern if modules are separated into microservices.

The ADR focuses on structuring the system to improve module autonomy and loose coupling, which are aspects of maintainability related to modularity and ease of change. It does not primarily address performance, security, or other quality attributes. The decision to have an IoC container per module is about making the system easier to modify and maintain by reducing coupling between modules.

The ADR focuses on implementing architecture tests to verify adherence to design rules and conventions, which directly relates to the ease and effectiveness of testing the system's architecture. It aims to provide quick feedback on architectural violations and improve verification processes, which is a core aspect of Testability. Although it mentions documentation and some maintainability benefits, the primary motivation is to enable effective testing of architectural constraints.

The ADR describes the decision to use Architecture Decision Records to document architectural decisions. This is about the process of recording decisions rather than any quality attribute of the system being built. There is no mention or implication of performance, reliability, security, maintainability, or any other quality attribute of the system itself.

The ADR focuses on choosing Express to reduce effort on non-domain specific problems and to leverage a well-documented, modular, and widely used framework. The emphasis is on ease of development, modularity via middleware, and flexibility in component choice, which are aspects of maintainability. There is no primary focus on performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes. The decision highlights maintainability benefits such as reduced duplication, community support, and easier component swapping.

The ADR focuses on using an external postcode lookup service that is free, supported, and monitored, emphasizing the reliability and availability of the service for resolving postcodes to coordinates. It also discusses consequences related to service unavailability and data accuracy (active postcodes only), which are aspects of reliability. There is no primary focus on performance, security, or maintainability, and the main concern is ensuring the system can reliably obtain accurate location data.

The ADR focuses on moving CPU-intensive geo-location search processing to a separate application to prevent blocking the web server and to allow scaling by adding more containers. The primary motivation is to handle increased load and maintain responsiveness under high demand, which aligns with Scalability. Although performance and reliability aspects are mentioned, the core decision is about scaling processing capacity to handle load growth effectively. Maintainability is a secondary benefit but not the primary driver.

The ADR focuses on adding cache control headers to reduce server load and avoid unnecessary re-requests, which directly improves system response time and resource utilization. This aligns with the Performance category, as it aims to optimize efficiency and throughput. Although caching can also impact scalability, the primary motivation stated is reducing load and improving response times, which is a Performance concern. Other categories like Reliability or Security are not the focus here, and the ADR does not address maintainability or usability aspects.

The ADR focuses on using Prometheus to expose metrics for monitoring the application's health and KPIs, which directly relates to Observability. The goal is to infer the internal state of the system from external outputs (metrics) to enable monitoring and alerting. Although there is mention of a performance cost, the primary motivation is to improve system transparency and monitoring, not performance optimization itself.

The ADR focuses on removing caching to ensure up-to-date search results, which primarily affects response freshness and timeliness of data delivery, aspects related to Performance (response time and data freshness). Although caching also impacts scalability and reliability, the primary motivation is to avoid stale data and improve the timeliness of information, which aligns best with Performance. Other categories like Reliability or Scalability are less relevant since the decision is about data freshness rather than fault tolerance or load handling.

The ADR focuses on adding basic authentication to test environments to control access and prevent unauthorized access, which directly relates to the security attribute, specifically access control and confidentiality. Although the credentials are not secret, the main goal is to create a barrier to unauthorized or unintended access, including bots. Other categories like Maintainability or Usability are not the primary focus here, and the decision is not about performance, scalability, or reliability.

The ADR focuses on distinguishing bot and automated check traffic from real user traffic to improve the accuracy of monitoring and analysis of user behavior. This is primarily about improving the system's observability by enabling better inference of internal states (real user activity) from external outputs (traffic data). It is not about performance, security, or other attributes. Although it relates to data filtering, the core motivation is to improve monitoring and understanding of system usage, which aligns with Observability.

The ADR focuses on using a consistent external service (postcodes.io) for reverse geocoding and place lookups, emphasizing interoperability and reuse of the existing API client. This relates primarily to system compatibility with external services and data sources. There is no mention of performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes as the main driver. The decision is about integrating with an external system consistently, which fits Compatibility best. Other categories like Maintainability or Portability are less relevant since the focus is on using the same service rather than ease of change or environment transfer.

The ADR focuses on adding metadata to enable a search box directly within Google, which improves user experience by allowing users to search the site more conveniently from Google. This primarily impacts usability by enhancing accessibility and user interaction. There is no indication that the decision is motivated by performance, security, or other quality attributes.

The ADR focuses on handling vulnerabilities in dependencies and the decision to remove Snyk is motivated by managing security risks related to vulnerabilities. The replacement tools (Greenkeeper and GitHub vulnerability subscriptions) are intended to maintain visibility and management of security issues. Although the ADR mentions build failures and overhead, the core concern is about protecting the system from vulnerabilities, which is a security attribute. Other categories like Maintainability or Performance are less relevant since the decision is not about ease of change or efficiency but about vulnerability management.

The ADR focuses on removing redundant code to make the code base cleaner and clearer, which improves the ease of modification and understanding of the system. There is no mention or implication of performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes related to system runtime behavior or user experience. The primary motivation is improving the internal structure and clarity of the system, which aligns with Maintainability.

The ADR focuses on using Azure Search API instead of maintaining Elasticsearch infrastructure. This decision is primarily motivated by reducing maintenance overhead and simplifying infrastructure management, which relates to Maintainability (ease of modification and management). There is no explicit mention of performance, scalability, or security improvements as the primary goal. The decision is about reducing operational complexity and maintenance burden.

The ADR focuses on providing an info page to aid debugging by showing the deployed version and application time in UTC, which improves the ability to monitor and understand the system's internal state from external outputs. This aligns with Observability. It is not about performance, security, or maintainability, but about runtime transparency and monitoring.

The ADR describes a change in the URL path structure for consistency with organizational information architecture plans. It focuses on what the system does (URL structure) without mentioning or implying any quality attributes such as performance, security, maintainability, or scalability. The decision is about functional organization rather than how well the system performs or behaves.

The ADR focuses on improving navigation and simplifying the user interface by updating links and removing redundant ones, which directly impacts user experience and ease of use. There is no mention of performance, security, maintainability, or other quality attributes. The primary motivation is to make the system easier and more intuitive to use, which aligns with Usability.

The ADR describes the decision to use Architecture Decision Records to document architectural decisions. This is about the process of documenting decisions rather than any quality attribute of the system being built. There is no mention or implication of performance, reliability, security, maintainability, or any other quality attribute of the system itself.

The ADR focuses on choosing an authentication mechanism (Devise with Magic Links) primarily to ensure secure user authentication and confidence in the app's security. The main motivation is protecting user access and data, which aligns with the Security quality attribute. Although maintainability and other aspects are mentioned, the core decision is about securing authentication.

The ADR describes the initial data model and application structure, focusing on what data entities exist and their relationships. It does not mention or imply any quality attributes such as performance, security, maintainability, or scalability. The decision is about the functional design of the data model rather than how well the system performs or other non-functional aspects.

The ADR primarily focuses on the architectural decision between microservices and monolith with the main motivation being ease of development, deployment, and maintainability of the codebase. It emphasizes structuring the application well to avoid complexity and maintain clear boundaries, and investing in fast tests to avoid slowdown in development. These concerns relate to the ease and efficiency of modifying and understanding the system, which aligns with Maintainability. Although scalability and performance are mentioned, they are explicitly considered less relevant or not beneficial in this context. There is no primary focus on runtime performance, reliability, security, or other quality attributes.

The ADR focuses on the internal organization and modular structure of the application to facilitate ease of change and clear separation of concerns. It describes how the application is divided into components and layers to improve code organization and maintainability. There is no mention of performance, scalability, security, or other quality attributes. The primary motivation is to make the system easier to understand and modify, which aligns with Maintainability.

The ADR primarily focuses on ensuring the Apply Service can function independently of the Find Service by creating local copies of data. This decision is motivated by the need to reduce dependency on the Find Service, thus improving fault tolerance and availability of the Apply Service. Although performance (faster lookups) and maintainability (control over local models) are mentioned, the core motivation is reliability through decoupling and resilience to Find Service unavailability.

The ADR primarily focuses on the user experience and usability issues introduced by integrating with the Enterprise API Management Gateway, such as confusing user experience, managing multiple tokens, and user overhead. While there are mentions of security and manageability concerns, the core motivation is the negative impact on users' ability to effectively and efficiently use the system's API access mechanisms. Other categories like Security or Maintainability are secondary and not the main driver of the decision.

The ADR focuses on how to evolve the API without breaking existing clients, specifically addressing backward compatibility and interoperability concerns with different vendor integrations. The main motivation is to allow API extensions without causing issues for clients that do not expect or cannot handle new fields, which is a classic compatibility concern. Although there are mentions of versioning and customization, the core issue is maintaining API compatibility across versions and clients. Other categories like Maintainability or Performance are not the focus here, as the decision is about API evolution strategy rather than internal code structure or efficiency. Security, Scalability, and others are not relevant to the primary concern described.

The ADR focuses on implementing asynchronous and scheduled jobs to ensure reliable execution of time-dependent business rules and background processing. It emphasizes fault tolerance through automatic retries of failed jobs and the need for supervision and restarting of processes to maintain continuous operation. While scalability and maintainability aspects are mentioned, the primary motivation is to ensure the system performs its functions reliably under stated conditions.

The ADR focuses on the trade-offs between session management approaches with respect to session invalidation and protection against unauthorized access. The main concern is about session security, including confidentiality (encrypted cookies) and the risk of session reuse or remote sign-out capabilities. Although performance and infrastructure considerations are mentioned, the primary motivation is security-related.

The ADR focuses on protecting sensitive diversity data from unauthorized access, considering risks like unauthorized viewing, SQL injection, accidental data exposure, and operational security breaches. The primary motivation is to ensure confidentiality, access control, and auditing of sensitive information, which aligns with the Security quality attribute. Although operational complexity and performance are mentioned, they are secondary to the core concern of protecting sensitive data access.

The ADR is primarily motivated by improving the security of the support interface by ensuring that only authorized users with verified email access (and thus 2FA) can access the system. The main concerns addressed are unauthorized access and ensuring that only current employees retain access, which are classic security concerns related to access control and authentication. Other categories like Usability or Maintainability are mentioned as considerations but are secondary to the core goal of enhancing security. Performance, Scalability, and others are not relevant here as the focus is on protecting information and controlling access.

The ADR focuses on handling invalid course option states to prevent submission errors and ensure the system behaves correctly under these conditions, which relates to the system's reliability in performing its functions under stated conditions. It addresses fault tolerance by managing cases where course options become invalid and ensuring consistent application behavior. Other categories like Performance or Usability are less relevant since the decision is not about speed or user interface improvements. Maintainability is not the focus as the ADR does not discuss ease of modification. Scalability, Security, Observability, Testability, Portability, and Compatibility are not primary concerns here.

The ADR focuses on the system's alerting and monitoring strategy, specifically on how internal states and issues are detected and reported externally to enable timely response. This is a clear case of Observability, as it deals with monitoring, alerting, and diagnosing system health and failures. Although reliability is related, the primary concern here is about detecting and understanding system state rather than ensuring uptime or fault tolerance directly. Other categories like Performance or Security are not the focus, and the ADR does not describe functional behavior alone, so Other/Only Functional Concern is not appropriate.

The ADR focuses on improving the user experience for candidates by allowing them to carry over their applications to the next recruitment cycle without re-filling the entire form. This decision is primarily motivated by making the system easier and more convenient to use for candidates, which aligns with Usability. There is no indication that the decision is primarily about performance, security, reliability, or other quality attributes. Although the decision involves data copying and state management, these are functional or usability concerns rather than maintainability or compatibility. Therefore, Usability is the best fit.

The ADR focuses on the tradeoff between database structure complexity and code complexity, choosing a JSON blob to reduce code complexity and encapsulate serialization logic. This is primarily about ease of modification and managing code complexity, which aligns with Maintainability. Although there is some mention of domain structure and data representation, the core decision is about simplifying code impact rather than performance, scalability, or other attributes. Other categories like Performance, Scalability, or Compatibility are not the focus here, and the decision is not about functional behavior but about how the system is structured internally for easier change and reduced complexity.

The ADR focuses on ensuring the accuracy of the updated_at timestamp on ApplicationChoices to prevent consumers from missing changes or processing duplicates. This is primarily about the system performing its function correctly and reliably under stated conditions, avoiding false positives and false negatives in change detection, which aligns with Reliability. Although there is some mention of maintainability aspects (like specs to keep the whitelist updated), the core motivation is to ensure correct and reliable behavior of the system's data updates, not ease of change or development process. Performance, Security, Scalability, and other categories are not the focus here.

The ADR focuses on ensuring that each qualification entity exposed by the API has a globally unique identifier, which is crucial for interoperability and correct identification by external vendor systems consuming the API. The primary motivation is to maintain backward compatibility and consistent identification across systems, which aligns with the Compatibility quality attribute. Although uniqueness of IDs can impact reliability or maintainability, the core concern here is about consistent data exchange and system interoperability via the API. Other categories like Performance, Security, or Scalability are not the focus, and while Maintainability is somewhat involved, it is secondary to the compatibility goal.

The ADR focuses on improving the testing approach for JavaScript integration by enabling system specs that run JavaScript in a headless browser environment. The primary motivation is to enhance the effectiveness and coverage of tests, ensuring that JavaScript and Rails-generated HTML interplay is properly tested. This directly relates to the quality attribute of Testability, as it improves the ability to verify and validate the system's behavior. Although there is mention of CI slowdown (Performance) and installation requirements (Portability), these are secondary concerns and not the primary driver of the decision.

The ADR focuses on the choice of a styling library primarily motivated by ease of use, theming support, code splitting, and longevity, which relate to how maintainable and manageable the styling code is over time. It does not primarily address performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes. The decision is about improving developer experience and code organization, which aligns with Maintainability.

The ADR focuses on using TypeScript primarily for type checking, built-in documentation, and improved maintainability, which are aspects related to ease of modification and code quality. It also mentions making the project more friendly to contributors, which aligns with maintainability. There is no mention of performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes as the primary motivation.

The ADR focuses on the organization of the codebase into a single NPM package versus multiple packages, which primarily affects the ease of development and maintainability of the system. It mentions simpler setup and quicker development, which are aspects of maintainability such as modularity and developer efficiency. There is no mention or implication of performance, scalability, security, or other quality attributes related to the system's runtime behavior or user experience.

The ADR focuses on using Storybook, a tool that allows users (design team) to view UI components in isolation and in different states, which primarily improves the usability and user experience of the design and development process. Although it indirectly supports maintainability by helping component reuse and understanding, the primary motivation is to enhance the effectiveness and satisfaction of users interacting with the components.

The ADR focuses on organizing the codebase into a monorepo structure using tools like Lerna and Yarn Workspaces to efficiently manage multiple packages. This primarily addresses maintainability concerns such as modularity, code organization, and ease of modification. There is no mention of performance, scalability, security, or other quality attributes related to the system's runtime behavior or user experience. The decision is about how the code is structured and managed, which aligns with Maintainability.

The ADR focuses on supporting different module import systems (CommonJS, ES Modules, UMD) to ensure broad compatibility with various application types and environments. The primary motivation is interoperability and the ability to exchange information and function correctly in different runtime contexts, which aligns with the Compatibility quality attribute. Although there are mentions of performance-related features like tree-shaking, the core decision is about module system support and interoperability rather than performance optimization. Other categories like Portability or Performance are less fitting because the decision is not about running on different platforms or optimizing speed, but about working with different module systems and environments.

The ADR focuses on the organization and structure of the codebase and compiled package to support modularity and ease of importing individual components. This primarily improves maintainability by making the system easier to understand, modify, and extend. Although there is mention of supporting different module formats (esm, umd, cjs), the core decision is about directory and package structure rather than performance or compatibility. Compatibility is a minor consideration but not the primary goal, as the emphasis is on internal organization and modularity.

The ADR focuses on evaluating existing React component libraries primarily to decide whether to extend them or build a new library. The key quality attribute is Maintainability, as the decision is motivated by the ease of modification, extensibility, and customization (themeability) of the component libraries. The ADR discusses criteria like theme support, CSS customization, and maintenance status, which relate to how easily the system can be modified and extended. Other categories like Performance, Security, or Scalability are not the focus here. Although accessibility and other attributes are mentioned, they are secondary to the core decision about maintainability and extensibility of the component libraries.

The ADR focuses on testing accessibility of UI components, which directly relates to the usability quality attribute, specifically accessibility and user experience. The decision is about how to ensure the system can be used effectively by users with accessibility needs. Other categories like Testability are relevant but secondary, as the primary goal is improving usability through accessibility testing.

The ADR focuses on separating business logic from Android framework classes to enable unit testing on the JVM rather than the Android VM. The primary motivation is to facilitate a fast feedback loop through easier and more effective testing of UI controllers by using RxJava streams and MVI architecture. This is a clear focus on improving the testability of the system. Other categories like Maintainability or Performance are less relevant here since the ADR does not primarily address ease of change or runtime efficiency, but rather the ability to test the system components effectively.

The ADR focuses on improving the user experience when interacting with bottom sheets that include input text fields, specifically addressing the issue of the on-screen keyboard covering content. The decision to use an Activity instead of a Fragment is motivated by the need to better align the UI above the keyboard, enhancing usability. Although there is a mention of a missing drag-to-dismiss feature, the primary concern is the user interface behavior and interaction, which falls under Usability. Other categories like Performance, Reliability, or Maintainability are not the main focus here, as the ADR does not discuss efficiency, fault tolerance, or ease of modification. Compatibility and Portability are also not relevant since the decision is about UI behavior rather than system interoperability or environment transferability.

The ADR focuses on the trade-off between enforcing data integrity at the database level (via foreign keys) versus allowing potential orphaned records due to distributed, offline data synchronization. The primary concern is maintaining system reliability in the face of partial data availability and network failures, accepting some loss of strict data integrity to avoid system failures. This relates to fault tolerance and recoverability aspects of Reliability. Although data integrity is a functional concern, the decision to relax foreign keys to handle offline scenarios and avoid failures under stated conditions aligns with Reliability. Other categories like Maintainability or Performance are less relevant since the decision is not about ease of change or efficiency, and Security or Scalability are not the focus here.

The ADR focuses on ensuring data consistency and conflict resolution between client and server copies, which are aspects of reliability, specifically fault tolerance and data integrity under offline and syncing conditions. The use of UUIDs to guarantee unique identifiers also supports reliable identification of records. Although there is a mention of performance trade-offs (UUIDs being slower and larger), the primary motivation is to maintain correctness and consistency of data, which aligns with Reliability. Other categories like Performance or Scalability are less relevant since the main concern is correctness and conflict resolution, not speed or load handling. Security is not the focus despite dealing with PHI, as the decision is about data source of truth and ID uniqueness rather than access control or confidentiality.

The ADR focuses on choosing a navigation system for the user interface that simplifies screen transitions and reduces complexity and bugs related to lifecycle synchronization. The primary motivation is improving the user experience by making navigation smoother, easier to manage, and less error-prone, which aligns with Usability. Although there are implications for maintainability (due to avoiding fragments and using a third-party library), the core decision is about how users interact with the system's UI and navigation flow. Performance, Reliability, and other categories are less relevant since the ADR does not emphasize speed, fault tolerance, or security aspects.

The ADR addresses forward compatibility of enumerated values between different app versions and the server, ensuring that new enum values can be handled gracefully by older versions without data loss or corruption. The primary motivation is to maintain interoperability and data consistency across different system versions and components, which aligns with Compatibility. Although there are implications for Maintainability (due to the custom infrastructure) and Reliability (data integrity), the core concern is about system interoperability and version compatibility.

The ADR focuses on separating presentation and business logic to improve testability and maintainability of the screen architecture. It emphasizes modularity, explicit state management, and ease of migration, all of which are aspects of maintainability. Although testability is mentioned, it is a sub-aspect of maintainability here, as the main goal is to improve the structure and ease of change of the system. There is no primary focus on performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes.

The ADR focuses on improving the architecture to separate concerns, making components smaller and more focused, easier to test and maintain. It emphasizes modularity, testability, and reducing complexity for onboarding and refactoring. Although it mentions RxJava usage and state management, the primary motivation is to improve the ease of change and maintainability of the system rather than performance, scalability, or other attributes.

The ADR focuses on migrating to Material Design Components to better align with design specifications and improve theming and styling capabilities of UI components. The primary motivation is to enhance the user interface's consistency, appearance, and ease of use, which relates to Usability. Although there are some maintainability aspects (like reducing button types), the core driver is improving the user experience through better design component support. There is no emphasis on performance, security, scalability, or other quality attributes.

The ADR focuses on improving type safety in dependency injection by migrating from using string-based @Named annotations to type-safe @Qualifier annotations. This change primarily aims to reduce developer errors and improve code quality and maintainability, rather than affecting performance, security, or other quality attributes. The decision is about how the system is structured and maintained, not about runtime behavior or functional capabilities.

The ADR primarily focuses on improving the navigation framework to make it easier to build, maintain, and incrementally migrate screens. It addresses modularity by encapsulating navigation logic in a Router, supports lifecycle integration, and reduces friction in building screens with modals. While it touches on usability aspects like layout editor previews and lifecycle support, the core motivation is to improve the ease of modification, integration, and incremental migration of the navigation system, which aligns best with Maintainability. Performance, Scalability, Security, and other categories are not the main focus here.

The ADR is primarily motivated by the need to measure and improve the performance of SQL queries in the application. The goal is to collect performance data automatically to proactively identify and fix slow queries before they impact users. The approaches described focus on instrumentation and profiling to track query execution times, which directly relates to the Performance quality attribute. Other categories like Maintainability or Observability are less relevant since the core concern is about query execution efficiency rather than ease of change or monitoring for debugging.

The ADR focuses on profiling SQL query performance by measuring execution time and reporting it. The primary motivation is to capture and improve the performance characteristics of SQL queries. Although it involves code transformation and build tooling, the core concern is about measuring and improving system performance, specifically SQL query execution time. Other categories like Maintainability are secondary concerns related to tooling compatibility, but the main goal is performance profiling.

The ADR focuses on structuring CSS stylesheets and rules for print media in a way that improves the organization, modularity, and maintainability of the codebase. It discusses separating styles into different files and components, aiming for clear separation and ease of updates, which are key aspects of maintainability.
